justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what appears to be a current price near 306, with very little directional conviction. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the last observed price, adding only a slight positive drift consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations — essentially assuming no major overnight catalyst would materially shift prices. At the one-week horizon, I added a small additional drift to arrive at 307, reflecting the same logic but allowing slightly more time for mean-reverting tendencies and modest trend continuation to play out. At the one-month horizon, the 308 estimate continues this gentle upward slope, consistent with historical average monthly returns for broad equity indices, though the incremental increase is deliberately small given the high uncertainty at that horizon.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated using historical realized volatility for the underlying asset, which I treated as consistent with a broad equity index or ETF. Daily volatility in the range of roughly 0.7–1% annualized implied translates to narrow intervals at the one-day horizon, while the one-week and one-month intervals widen in proportion to the square root of time — a standard assumption when price changes approximate a random walk. The one-month interval spanning roughly plus or minus 26 points (about 8.5% of the price level) reflects the realistic range of outcomes over four weeks of market trading under normal conditions, drawing on typical index volatility in the low-to-mid teens on an annualized basis.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside these intervals. On the downside, a significant macroeconomic surprise — such as a sharp deterioration in employment data, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, an escalation in geopolitical conflict, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could easily drive prices 10–15% below my stated lower bounds over a one-month window. On the upside, a strongly positive inflation surprise, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could fuel a sharp rally beyond the upper bound.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normal market conditions with no regime change. Fat-tailed events — financial crises, pandemics, sudden liquidity shocks — are structurally underrepresented in symmetric confidence intervals derived from recent volatility estimates. In practice, realized distributions of equity returns have heavier tails than a normal approximation suggests, meaning the true probability of an extreme outcome at the one-month horizon is meaningfully higher than the stated 10% residual probability outside my 90% interval would imply.
